facts: Albania was the most isolated country in Europe under Enver Hoxha, who had several hundred thousand concrete bunkers built across the countryside; many still sit in fields and on beaches today.
Private cars were banned for ordinary citizens until 1991, so the country went from almost no traffic to full motorisation within a single generation.
The Albanian language forms its own independent branch of the Indo-European family, with no close living relatives.
Andorra has two heads of state at once: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain, an arrangement dating from 1278.
At 1,023 metres, Andorra la Vella is the highest capital city in Europe.
The country has no airport and no railway; every visitor arrives by road through the Pyrenees.
Austria borders eight countries, more than any other European state except Germany, Russia and Serbia.
Around 62% of the country lies within the Alps, which is why its population concentrates along the Danube in the flatter east.
Vienna draws most of its drinking water directly from Alpine springs through pipelines built in the 1870s.
Belarus is one of the flattest countries in Europe; its highest point is a hill barely taller than a 100-storey building.
Around a fifth of the country is forest and marshland, including Belovezhskaya Pushcha, one of the last primeval forests on the continent.
It is among the few European countries that never had a coastline at any point in its history.
Belgium has three official languages — Dutch, French and German — and a federal structure built around that divide.
Brussels hosts the headquarters of both the European Union and NATO.
The port of Antwerp is one of the largest in Europe and handles a substantial share of the continent's chemical trade.
Bosnia and Herzegovina has roughly 20 kilometres of coastline at Neum, which splits Croatia's territory in two.
The country has a three-member presidency, with one Bosniak, one Croat and one Serb member serving at the same time.
The 1984 Winter Olympics were held in Sarajevo; several of the venues were damaged during the siege of the city a decade later.
Musala is the highest peak in the whole Balkan Peninsula, not just in Bulgaria.
Plovdiv is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, with settlement traces going back some 8,000 years.
Bulgaria produces a large share of the world's rose oil, distilled in the Valley of the Roses near Kazanlak.
Croatia's coastline includes more than 1,200 islands, though fewer than 50 are permanently inhabited.
The country is shaped like a crescent, and its territory is interrupted near Neum by Bosnia and Herzegovina's short coastal strip.
The necktie descends from the scarves worn by Croatian mercenaries in 17th-century France — 'cravate' comes from 'Croat'.
Czechia has the highest beer consumption per person of any country in the world.
Charles University in Prague, founded in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe.
The country split peacefully from Slovakia on 1 January 1993 in what is usually called the Velvet Divorce.
Denmark proper consists of the Jutland peninsula and around 400 islands, roughly 70 of which are inhabited.
Its highest natural point is lower than many office buildings, making it one of the flattest countries in Europe.
The Kingdom of Denmark also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands, both self-governing.
Estonia was the first country to hold legally binding general elections over the internet, in 2005.
More than half the country is covered by forest, and it has over 2,000 islands in the Baltic Sea.
Estonian is closely related to Finnish and unrelated to the Indo-European languages spoken by most of its neighbours.
Finland has roughly 188,000 lakes, more relative to its size than any other country.
About a quarter of its territory lies north of the Arctic Circle, where the sun does not set for weeks in summer.
Finnish belongs to the Uralic family alongside Estonian and Hungarian, not to the Indo-European family.
Counting its overseas departments, France spans twelve time zones — more than any other country.
It is the most visited country in the world by international arrivals.
Because of French Guiana in South America, France's longest land border is with Brazil.
Germany borders nine countries, more than any other in Europe apart from Russia.
It was unified as a single nation state only in 1871, and divided again from 1949 until 1990.
Roughly a third of the country is forested, and it has more than 20,000 castles and fortified houses.
Greece has around 6,000 islands and islets, of which roughly 227 are inhabited.
No part of the country is more than about 137 kilometres from the sea.
Its merchant fleet is among the largest in the world by tonnage, despite the country's small population.
Lake Balaton is the largest lake in Central Europe and is sometimes called the Hungarian Sea.
Budapest was formed in 1873 by merging Buda and Óbuda on one bank of the Danube with Pest on the other.
Hungarian is a Uralic language, unrelated to the Slavic and Germanic tongues surrounding it.
Iceland sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so the island is slowly being pulled apart between two tectonic plates.
Almost all of its electricity and heating comes from hydro and geothermal sources.
The Althing, founded around 930, is often described as the oldest surviving parliament in the world.
Ireland has no native snakes, a fact folklore credits to Saint Patrick but which glaciation explains better.
The Great Famine of the 1840s cut the population by around a quarter through death and emigration, and it has still not returned to its pre-famine peak.
Its only land border is with Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom.
Italy completely surrounds two other sovereign states, San Marino and Vatican City.
It has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country.
Mount Etna in Sicily is the most active volcano in Europe and has been erupting on and off for at least 2,700 years.
Riga has one of the largest collections of Art Nouveau architecture of any city in the world.
Latvia is about half forest, one of the highest proportions in the European Union.
The Baltic Way of 1989 saw two million people form a human chain across Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
Liechtenstein is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, meaning every neighbour is landlocked too.
It has no airport and no army, having disbanded its forces in 1868.
The country produces more registered companies than it has residents.
Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, in March 1990.
The medieval Grand Duchy of Lithuania was at one point the largest state in Europe.
Its border with Russia is with Kaliningrad, an exclave separated from the rest of the country.
Luxembourg is the world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy, a title that once applied to several European states.
It has among the highest GDP per capita of any country, driven largely by banking and investment funds.
In 2020 it became the first country to make all public transport free nationwide.
Malta is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, with the whole nation smaller than many cities.
Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and the only one that is an official EU language.
The Ġgantija temples on Gozo predate both Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids.
Moldova's Cricova and Mileștii Mici cellars hold some of the largest wine collections in the world, stored in tunnels tens of kilometres long.
The country is landlocked apart from a few hundred metres of Danube frontage at Giurgiulești, which gives it a river port.
Transnistria, a strip east of the Dniester, has operated outside government control since 1992.
Monaco is the second smallest country in the world and the most densely populated.
It has expanded its territory by around 20% since the 1960s by reclaiming land from the sea.
The Monaco Grand Prix is run on public streets that are returned to normal traffic within days.
Montenegro restored its independence in 2006 after a referendum ended its union with Serbia.
The Bay of Kotor is a deeply indented inlet often described, inaccurately but persistently, as Europe's southernmost fjord.
The country uses the euro despite never having been a member of the European Union.
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by an extensive system of dikes and pumps.
Amsterdam is the constitutional capital, but the government, parliament and royal residence are in The Hague.
The country is one of the world's largest agricultural exporters despite its small size, largely through greenhouse horticulture.
The country added 'North' to its name in 2019 to settle a long dispute with Greece over the name Macedonia.
Lake Ohrid, shared with Albania, is among the oldest and deepest lakes in Europe.
It is landlocked and mountainous, with more than fifty peaks above 2,000 metres.
Norway's coastline, counting fjords and islands, runs to well over 100,000 kilometres.
Its sovereign wealth fund, built on North Sea oil, is the largest in the world.
Svalbard, far to the north, is Norwegian territory but open to citizens of all treaty signatories to live and work.
Poland disappeared from the map entirely between 1795 and 1918, partitioned between three empires.
Białowieża Forest on the Belarusian border is one of the last remaining fragments of Europe's primeval lowland forest.
Warsaw's old town was rebuilt almost from scratch after 1945, using paintings as reference, and is now a World Heritage Site.
Portugal's mainland border with Spain is one of the oldest continuously settled borders in Europe, largely fixed since 1297.
The country produces about half the world's cork, harvested from oak bark without felling the trees.
Its highest point is not on the mainland but on Pico Island in the Azores, over 1,500 kilometres out in the Atlantic.
The Danube Delta, where the river meets the Black Sea, is the best-preserved river delta in Europe.
Romanian is a Romance language, descended from Latin, surrounded on almost all sides by Slavic and Hungarian speakers.
The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is among the heaviest buildings ever constructed.
Russia spans eleven time zones and borders fourteen countries, both world records.
It is larger than Pluto's surface area, and covers about an eighth of the world's inhabited land.
Lake Baikal in Siberia holds roughly a fifth of all unfrozen fresh water on Earth.
San Marino claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and the oldest republic, traditionally founded in 301.
It is entirely surrounded by Italy and has never had a coastline.
The country has two heads of state, the Captains Regent, who serve six-month terms together.
Serbia lost its coastline when Montenegro voted for independence in 2006.
Belgrade sits where the Sava meets the Danube and has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times.
The country is a major exporter of raspberries, supplying a large share of the world's frozen crop.
Bratislava is the only national capital that borders two other countries, Austria and Hungary.
Slovakia has one of the highest numbers of castles and châteaux per person in the world.
It became an independent state for the first time in the modern era in 1993, on splitting from Czechia.
More than half of Slovenia is forested, one of the highest shares in Europe.
The word 'karst', used worldwide for limestone cave landscapes, comes from Slovenia's Kras region.
Its coastline on the Adriatic is only about 47 kilometres long.
Spain borders Morocco by land at the enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla on the African coast.
Its highest point, Teide, is on Tenerife in the Canary Islands rather than the mainland.
Madrid, at around 650 metres, is the highest capital city in the European Union.
Sweden has around 267,000 islands, more than any other country, though most are uninhabited.
The right of public access, allmansrätten, lets anyone walk and camp on most land regardless of who owns it.
It has not fought a war since 1814, one of the longest unbroken stretches of peace of any country.
Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
It is a direct democracy where citizens vote on referendums several times a year, and it joined the UN only in 2002.
Bern is the seat of government, but the country has no formally designated capital city in its constitution.
Ukraine is the largest country lying entirely within Europe, ahead of France and Spain.
Its chernozem black soils are among the most fertile in the world, making it a major grain exporter.
Kyiv is one of the oldest cities in Eastern Europe, a major centre by the 10th century.
The United Kingdom is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Its only land border is with Ireland, running across the island of Ireland.
It has no single codified constitution, relying instead on statute, convention and case law.
Vatican City is the smallest sovereign state in the world, at about 0.49 square kilometres.
It is an elective absolute monarchy, with the Pope as head of state chosen by the College of Cardinals.
Almost all of its residents are clergy or Swiss Guards, and citizenship is generally tied to holding office rather than birth.
